questions.q: Which two rules should guide the level of autonomy you give a new automation?
options: Start at the highest level you can, then step down if problems appear
Use full autonomy for internal tasks and review only for customer ones
Pick the level that saves the most time, then add review later on
Start one level lower than you think, and promote with evidence
questions.explain: Start one level lower than you think you need, and promote with evidence, not optimism, by deciding in advance what proof you need before moving up a level.

questions.q: A candidate task scores 26 out of 30, but its cost-of-a-mistake score is 2 because errors could cause financial harm. How should you proceed?
options: Run it fully autonomously, since the total is well above 22
Automate it, but have a human approve every single output
Drop it, since a score of 2 rules a task out completely
Automate it and spot-check a random sample each week
questions.explain: The special rule says that if cost of a mistake scores 1 or 2, a human must approve every output, no matter how high the total score is.

questions.q: A task runs 300 times a month. Automating it saves 4 minutes per run, but someone still spends 1 minute reviewing each output. Roughly what is the real monthly saving before upkeep and build time?
questions.explain: Hours saved are 300 x 4 / 60 = 20, and review time is 300 x 1 / 60 = 5 hours to subtract. That leaves about 15 hours before upkeep and build time.
